items.explanation: In Robert Browning's dramatic monologues, 'Abt Vogler' is spoken by an eighteenth-century German musician/organist (I-2), 'Andrea del Sarto' by a Renaissance painter/artist (II-4), 'Childe Roland to the Dark Tower Came' by a medieval knight on a quest (III-1), and 'Cleon' by a classical Greek poet (IV-3).

structured.lead: Which one of Brecht's works was intended to lampoon the conventional sentimental musical but the public lapped up the work's sentiment and missed the humour ?
structured.options_hint: Man is Man Three Penny Opera The Mother

items.explanation: Bertolt Brecht and composer Kurt Weill wrote The Threepenny Opera (Die Dreigroschenoper, 1928)—an adaptation of John Gay's The Beggar's Opera—to satirize bourgeois capitalism and conventional sentimental musicals, though audiences ironically embraced its catchy songs and sentiment.

structured.options_hint: Vox Populi Epicurus Senior Democritus Ju

items.explanation: Oxford scholar Robert Burton published his encyclopedic work The Anatomy of Melancholy (1621) under the pseudonym 'Democritus Junior,' after the ancient Greek 'laughing philosopher' Democritus of Abdera who dissected animals to discover the seat of black bile.

items.title: Q5 · June 2013 (Paper III)
items.meta: Roman Augustan (Golden Age) · Unit II: Poetry · Horace
items.stem: Horace Walpole's novel The Castle of Otranto tells the story of

structured.lead: Horace Walpole's novel The Castle of Otranto tells the story of
structured.options_hint: A defiant and heartless tyrant who kills

options: A defiant and heartless tyrant who kills his own son mercilessly
An usurper and a tyrant who kills his own daughter by mistake
A castle that collapses and crushes the young and sickly prince to death
A tyrant who retires to a monastery at the end and lives happily ever after with his queen
items.explanation: Horace Walpole's The Castle of Otranto (1764), the first English Gothic novel, centres on Manfred, the tyrannical usurper prince of Otranto, who in a jealous rage accidentally stabs his own daughter Matilda to death in a dark church, mistaking her for Isabella.

structured.lead:

The following list contains poems which illustrate this theme, with one exception. Identify the exception
structured.options_hint: Kubla Khan Confessions of an English Opi

options: Confessions of an English Opium Eater
items.explanation: As per the official UGC answer key, Samuel Taylor Coleridge's 'Kubla Khan' (1816) is identified as the exception because its dream vision celebrates the ecstatic, godlike power of poetic creation ('a miracle of rare device'), whereas works like De Quincey's Confessions and Keats's The Fall of Hyperion emphasize anguished, nightmare visions.

items.stem: The book was for many years banned for obscenity in Britain and the United States. The central character is a Catholic Jew in Ireland. The author claimed that the book is meant to make you laugh. Which is this book ?

structured.lead:

United States. The central character is
a Catholic Jew in Ireland. The author claimed that the book is meant to make you laugh. Which is this book ?
structured.options_hint: The Picture of Dorian Grey Herzog Portno

items.explanation: James Joyce's modernist masterpiece Ulysses (1922) centres on Leopold Bloom—a Dublin advertising canvasser of Jewish heritage baptized into both the Protestant and Catholic churches—on June 16, 1904. Banned for obscenity in the US and UK for years, Joyce remarked that there is not a serious line in it.

Solutions ?
structured.options_hint: The play centres around a middle class H

options: The play centres around a middle class Hindu family during a communal riot
It is concerned with homosexual relationship
It promotes religious pluralism in South Asia
items.explanation: Mahesh Dattani's Sahitya Akademi Award-winning play Final Solutions (1993) examines deep-seated Hindu-Muslim communal prejudice when two Muslim youths seek shelter in the home of a middle-class Hindu family during a riot. Homosexual relationships are explored in Dattani's other plays such as On a Muggy Night in Mumbai.

items.title: Q11 · June 2013 (Paper III)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII
items.stem: According to Bakhtin the idea of the Carnivalesque represents the following characteristics except

structured.lead:
According to Bakhtin the idea of the
Carnivalesque represents the following characteristics except
structured.options_hint: a liberation from the prevailing truth a

options: a liberation from the prevailing truth and established order
a harking back to the past
emphasis on play, parody, pleasure and the body
the suspension of all hierarchical rank, principles, norms and prohibitions
items.explanation: In Rabelais and His World (1965), Russian theorist Mikhail Bakhtin defines the 'carnivalesque' as a subversive mode marked by bodily grotesque realism, parody, laughter, and the temporary suspension of official hierarchies and dogmas, rather than a nostalgic harking back to the past.

items.title: Q12 · June 2013 (Paper III)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Patrick White
items.stem: Which of the following statements is not true of Patrick White ?

structured.lead: Which of the following statements is not true of Patrick White ?
structured.options_hint: He is remembered today for his epic and

options: He is remembered today for his epic and psychological narrative art
He is the only Australian to receive the Nobel Prize in literature
He pioneered a new fictional landscape and introduced a new continent in literature
His style is noted for lucidity and simplicity
items.explanation: While Patrick White won the 1973 Nobel Prize in Literature with the citation that he 'introduced a new continent into literature,' South African-born Nobel laureate J. M. Coetzee (2003) became an Australian citizen in 2006, making White no longer the only Australian Nobel laureate (note also that White's prose is famously dense rather than simple).

items.title: Q13 · June 2013 (Paper III)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: Conventional scholarship dates 'Early Modern English' as beginning around

structured.lead: Conventional scholarship dates 'Early Modern English' as beginning around

items.explanation: Historical linguistics conventionally divides the history of English into Old English (c. 450–1100), Middle English (c. 1100–1500), Early Modern English (c. 1500–1800, beginning around the introduction of printing and the Great Vowel Shift), and Late Modern English (c. 1800–present).

items.explanation: In R. K. Narayan's The Man-Eater of Malgudi (1961), the pious printer Sastri speaks these words to Nataraj about the tyrannical, bullying taxidermist H. Vasu. Comparing Vasu to the mythological demon Bhasmasura, Sastri's prophecy comes true when Vasu accidentally kills himself by slapping a mosquito on his own forehead.

items.title: Q15 · June 2013 (Paper III)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII
items.stem: Which of the following is not true of post-structuralism ?

structured.lead: Which of the following is not true of post-structuralism ?
structured.options_hint: It seeks to undermine the idea that mean

options: It seeks to undermine the idea that meaning pre-exists its linguistic expression
There can be no meaning which is not formulated and no language formulation reaches anywhere beyond language
There is no a-textual 'origin' of a text
Every sign refers to every other sign adequately
items.explanation: Post-structuralism rejects the structuralist assumption of a stable, closed system of signs. Through Jacques Derrida's concept of différance, post-structuralists argue that meaning is endlessly deferred along a chain of signifiers, so no sign ever refers to another sign with complete or adequate closure.

items.title: Q16 · June 2013 (Paper III)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Wole Soyinka

structured.lead:
Which of the following statements is not true of Wole Soyinka's The
Swamp Dwellers ?
structured.options_hint: It talks about the family, the extended

options: It talks about the family, the extended family in the African society
It is a confrontation between the traditional and modern society
It talks about the migration of people, crossing of borders and diasporic anguish
It is a comment about the city, urban, modern and the country rural, the swamp, the ancient
items.explanation: Wole Soyinka's early play The Swamp Dwellers (1958) dramatizes the clash between rural tradition in a Nigerian delta village and modern urban corruption in Lagos through the elderly couple Makuri and Alu, their disillusioned son Igwezu, and a blind northern beggar, rather than international migration and diasporic anguish.

items.stem:
Assertion (A) : A quarto refers to a text in which each leaf was a quarter the size of the original sheet.
Reason (R) : Because eight pages of text were printed on large sheets of paper, which were then folded four times to produce four leaves.
In the context of the two statements, which one of the following is correct ?

structured.lead: Given below are two statements:

statements.label: Assertion (A)
statements.text: A quarto refers to a text in which each leaf was a quarter the size of the original sheet.

statements.label: Reason (R)
statements.text: Because eight pages of text were printed on large sheets of paper, which were then folded four times to produce four leaves. In the context of the two statements, which one of the following is correct ?

structured.options_hint: (A) is correct but (R) is wrong. Both (A

items.explanation: Assertion (A) is true because a quarto leaf is one-fourth the size of the original printer's sheet. Reason (R) is false because to produce four leaves (eight pages), the sheet is folded twice (not four times).

items.title: Q20 · June 2013 (Paper III)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: The purpose of the Pre-Raphaelites was primarily to promote

structured.lead: The purpose of the Pre-Raphaelites was primarily to promote
structured.options_hint: complexity and ambivalence in art and li

options: complexity and ambivalence in art and literature
simplicity and naturalness in art and literature
symbolic and classical modes in art and literature
psychological and mythic modes in art and literature
items.explanation: Founded in 1848 by Dante Gabriel Rossetti, William Holman Hunt, and John Everett Millais, the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood sought to reject the artificial academic conventions of Victorian art and return to the simplicity, naturalness, and vivid fidelity to nature found in Italian art before Raphael.

structured.options_hint: Hamlet Women Beware Women The Spanish Tr

items.explanation: While the official UGC key marks Hamlet, all four plays actually feature metatheatrical performances—The Mousetrap in Hamlet, the fatal wedding masque in Middleton's Women Beware Women, Soliman and Perseda in Kyd's The Spanish Tragedy, and Pyramus and Thisbe in A Midsummer Night's Dream.

options: It seeks to expose the problematic nature of 'centered' discourses

items.explanation: Developed by Jacques Derrida in works like Of Grammatology (1967) and Writing and Difference (1967), deconstruction seeks to expose the internal contradictions and problematic assumptions of 'centered' (logocentric) discourses that rely on fixed origins or stable binary oppositions.

items.explanation: Spoken by Ferdinand in Act IV, Scene 2 of John Webster's The Duchess of Malfi (1614) upon seeing his murdered sister's body, these lines express his sudden, overwhelming shock and remorse as her twin. options: a second language learner makes educated guesses about word meanings in a text by recognizing cognates

items.title: Q72 · June 2013 (Paper III)

items.stem: Which of the following is not true of post-structuralism ?

structured.lead: Which of the following is not true of post-structuralism ?
structured.options_hint: It seeks to undermine the idea that mean

options: It seeks to undermine the idea that meaning pre-exists its linguistic expression
There can be no meaning which is not formulated and no language formulation reaches anywhere beyond language
There is no a-textual 'origin' of a text
Every sign refers to every other sign adequately
items.explanation: Post-structuralism rejects the structuralist view of language as a closed, stable system. Drawing on Jacques Derrida's concept of différance, it holds that meaning is endlessly deferred along a chain of signifiers, so no sign ever refers to every other sign with complete adequacy.

structured.lead: Which of the following secondlanguage learners would most likely acquire the second language more easily ?
structured.options_hint: a high school student who has been enrol

options: a high school student who has been enrolled in mandatory classes in the second language since elementary school
a visitor to a country where the second language is spoken; he interacts with hotel and restaurant personnel using the second language
a business person for whom fluency in the second language may lead to career advancement
an immigrant living in a country where the second language is spoken; he feels accepted by speakers of the second language
items.explanation: According to John Schumann's Acculturation Model and Stephen Krashen's Affective Filter Hypothesis in Second Language Acquisition, an immigrant living in the target-language country who feels socially accepted by native speakers experiences low social distance and a low affective filter, acquiring the language most easily.

structured.options_hint: Morton Hythloday Giles More

items.explanation: In Book I of Sir Thomas More's Utopia (1516), Thomas More himself, his humanist friend Peter Giles of Antwerp, and Cardinal John Morton (in whose household More served as a youth) are real historical figures, whereas the Portuguese traveller Raphael Hythloday ('speaker of nonsense') is wholly fictional.
